chunks: But if you are truthful, O you who exert yourself in describing your Lord,
then describe Gabriel, Michael, and the host of the near angels, in the chambers of holiness, perplexed, their minds bewildered as to how to define the Best of Creators.
For that which is perceived through qualities has forms and parts, and that which perishes when it reaches the end of its term by annihilation,
there is no god but He. He illuminated every darkness with His light, and darkened every light with His darkness.
ai.seo_question: How does Nahj al-Balagha use the angels to explain the limits of defining God?
ai.summary: Imam Ali employs the concept of *tanzih* (transcendence) by illustrating that even the highest angels, whose intellects are overwhelmed by the Divine presence, cannot circumscribe God's essence. This passage underscores the Shia theological principle that definition requires limits and parts, implying finitude, whereas God is beyond all attributes of creation. It concludes with a poetic affirmation of His absolute uniqueness, where His light illuminates all darkness and His essence surpasses all perception.

en.sayed-ali-raza: O you who exert yourself in describing Allāh if you are serious

then (first try to) describe Gabriel, Michael or the host of angels who are close (to Allāh) in the receptacles of sublimity; but their heads are bent downwards and their wits are perplexed as to how to assign limits (of definition) to the Highest Creator.
This is because those things can only be perceived through qualities which have shape and parts and which succumb to death after reaching the end of their times.
There is no god but He. He has lighted every darkness with His effulgence and has darkened every light with the darkness (of death).
